# Incident Report — NetSupport RAT Infection (2024-11-26)

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.11.26.183** |
| MAC address | **d0:57:7b:ce:fc:8b** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-B8TQK49** (NetBIOS name table also shows workgroup/computer name `NEMOTODES`; domain-joined to `nemotoads.health`, DC `NEMOTODES-DC.nemotoads.health` / 10.11.26.3) |
| Logged-in Windows user | **oboomwald** (from Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString, realm `NEMOTODES`/`NEMOTODES.HEALTH`) |

## 2. Malware Family

**NetSupport RAT** (malicious repurposing of the legitimate NetSupport Manager remote-access client).

**Attribution: signature-confirmed, and independently corroborated by protocol content.**
- Suricata/ETPRO fired direct signature matches: `ETPRO TROJAN NetSupport RAT CnC Activity`, `ETPRO TROJAN Malicious NetSupport Rat CnC Checkin`, `ET INFO NetSupport Remote Admin Checkin`, `ET INFO NetSupport Remote Admin Response`, `ET POLICY NetSupport GeoLocation Lookup Request`.
- Traffic to the C2 server carries the literal HTTP header `User-Agent: NetSupport Manager/1.3`.
- The exported HTTP bodies from the C2 stream show the actual NetSupport client protocol keywords in plaintext: `CMD=POLL / INFO=1 / ACK=1` (heartbeat) and `CMD=ENCD / ES=1 / DATA=<binary>` (encoded command/response channel) — this is the documented NetSupport Manager wire protocol, not a guess.

## 3. Timeline / Infection Vector

- 08:50:11–08:50:40 (local capture time, UTC+4): host resolves and connects over TLS to two suspicious domains flagged by ET as a "ZPHP" campaign: `classicgrand.com` (213.246.109.5) and `modandcrackedapk.com` (193.42.38.139, also flagged in TLS SNI). These are consistent with a fake "cracked APK/software" lure site — a known NetSupport RAT delivery vector (fake update/CAPTCHA pages). Content of these sessions is TLS-encrypted, so no dropped filename or hash is recoverable from the wire.
- 08:50:45: host performs a NetSupport geolocation lookup (`GET /location/loca.asp` to `geo.netsupportsoftware.com`, 104.26.1.231) — the RAT client initializing itself.
- 08:50:45 onward: host begins beaconing to the C2 with `User-Agent: NetSupport Manager/1.3`, POSTing to `http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm` on TCP/443 (plaintext HTTP over the port normally reserved for TLS — itself a detection indicator: `ET POLICY HTTP Request/POST on Unusual Port Possibly Hostile`).
- Beaconing continues at a steady ~60-second interval from **08:50:45 through 09:43:29** (58 check-ins observed in the capture), indicating an active, persistent RAT session for the duration of the capture.

## 4. Indicators of Compromise

**C2 endpoint (confirmed active RAT channel):**
- `194.180.191.64:443` (HTTP, not TLS) — POST `/fakeurl.htm`, User-Agent `NetSupport Manager/1.3`

**Malicious/suspicious domains (delivery stage):**
- `modandcrackedapk.com` → 193.42.38.139
- `classicgrand.com` → 213.246.109.5

**RAT-support infrastructure (used by the implant, not the initial lure):**
- `geo.netsupportsoftware.com` → 104.26.1.231, `GET /location/loca.asp`

**URLs observed:**
- `http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm` (C2 checkin, repeated)
- `http://geo.netsupportsoftware.com/location/loca.asp` (geolocation probe, returned coordinates `33.7488,-84.3877`)

**Files / hashes:**
- No malware binary, dropped filename, or file hash could be extracted from this capture. Both suspected delivery sessions (`classicgrand.com`, `modandcrackedapk.com`) are TLS-encrypted end to end, so the payload/installer is not visible in cleartext. The only cleartext artifacts recovered are the C2 protocol bodies (`fakeurl.htm` containing `CMD=POLL`/`CMD=ENCD` tokens) and the `loca.asp` geolocation response — neither is a transferred file with a computable SHA256.

## 5. Recommendation

Isolate DESKTOP-B8TQK49 (10.11.26.183) immediately, block 194.180.191.64, modandcrackedapk.com, and classicgrand.com at the perimeter, and image the host for offline analysis of the NetSupport client installation (`client32.exe`/`pcicapi.dll`/config `.ini` under `%ProgramFiles%\NetSupport\NetSupport Manager\` or similar) to recover the installer and hash it, since that artifact was not observable in this network capture alone.
